s-5.6-control-scope-detail.title: 5.6 Control Scope (continued): inputs, variance and trend analysis, baseline revisions
s-5.6-control-scope-detail.notes: Inputs detail: scope management plan (how scope is controlled), requirements management plan, change management plan (process for managing change), configuration management plan (configurable items, items needing formal change control, the control process), scope baseline and performance measurement baseline (compared with actual results, the latter when using earned value), lessons learned register, requirements documentation (detect deviation from agreed scope), RTM (impact of changes/deviations on objectives; requirement status), work performance data (number of change requests received and accepted, deliverables verified, validated and completed), OPAs (scope control policies, monitoring and reporting methods and templates). Variance analysis compares baseline to actual and decides whether the variance is within threshold or needs corrective/preventive action; trend analysis checks whether performance is improving or deteriorating over time; key aspects: the cause and degree of variance relative to the scope baseline and whether action is needed. WPI: correlated and contextualised scope performance vs baseline - categories of changes, scope variances and causes, schedule/cost impact, forecast scope performance. Change requests may target scope and schedule baselines or other components. Plan updates: scope management plan; scope, schedule, cost and performance measurement baselines updated in response to approved changes - and when variances are so severe that a revised baseline is needed to give a realistic basis for performance measurement. Document updates: lessons learned (causes of variances and corrective actions chosen), requirements documentation, RTM.

t-schedule-overview.title: Project Schedule Management overview: six processes, scheduling method/tool/model, trends, tailoring, agile
t-schedule-overview.section: 6 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figures 6-1, 6-2)
t-schedule-overview.notes: Processes to manage timely completion. 6.1 Plan Schedule Management (policies, procedures and documentation for planning, developing, managing, executing and controlling the schedule); 6.2 Define Activities (identify and document specific actions to produce deliverables); 6.3 Sequence Activities (identify and document relationships among activities); 6.4 Estimate Activity Durations (number of work periods to complete activities with estimated resources); 6.5 Develop Schedule (analyse sequences, durations, resource requirements and constraints to create the schedule model); 6.6 Control Schedule (monitor status, update the schedule, manage changes to the schedule baseline). Key concepts: the schedule is a detailed plan of how and when the project will deliver its scope, a communication tool, a way to manage expectations and a basis for performance reporting. The team selects a scheduling method (e.g., critical path or an agile approach), enters project-specific data (activities, dates, durations, resources, dependencies, constraints, calendars, milestones, lags) into a scheduling tool to create a schedule model, which generates the project schedule and presentations such as network diagrams, bar charts and activity lists (Figure 6-2). On small projects 6.2-6.5 are so tightly linked they act as one process done by one person quickly; presented separately because their tools differ. Keep the detailed schedule flexible for knowledge gained, risk understanding and value-added activities. Trends: adaptive planning; iterative scheduling with a backlog (rolling wave on adaptive life cycles; user stories prioritised and refined just before construction; time-boxed work; delivers incremental value; good when many teams build features with few dependencies; welcomes change); on-demand scheduling (Kanban; theory of constraints and lean pull concepts; limit work in progress to balance demand with throughput; pull from a backlog/queue as resources free up; suits incremental evolution in operational or sustainment settings with similarly sized tasks). Tailoring: life cycle approach; resource availability and productivity; project dimensions (complexity, technological uncertainty, novelty, pace, progress tracking such as EV, percent complete, stop-light indicators); technology support. Agile: short cycles with review and adaptation; large organisations may need long-term roadmaps and scaling factors (team size, geography, regulation, organisational and technical complexity), combining predictive, adaptive or hybrid techniques; the PM's role does not change, but the PM must know adaptive tools and techniques. ITTOs for 6.1-6.6 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 6-1.

t-6.1-plan-schedule.title: 6.1 Plan Schedule Management: the schedule management plan contents
t-6.1-plan-schedule.notes: Establish policies, procedures and documentation for the schedule; key benefit: guidance on how the schedule will be managed; once or at predefined points. Inputs: charter (summary milestone schedule); plan (scope management plan; development approach - shapes scheduling approach, estimating techniques, tools, control techniques); EEFs (culture and structure, team and physical resource availability and skills, scheduling software, tailoring guidelines, commercial databases such as standardised estimating data); OPAs (historical information and lessons learned, schedule policies and procedures, templates and forms, monitoring and reporting tools). Tools: expert judgment (schedule development, management and control; methodologies; software; industry); alternatives analysis (which methodology or combination, how detailed, rolling-wave wave length, review frequency - balancing detail against update effort); meetings. Output: schedule management plan (formal or informal, detailed or broad, with control thresholds), establishing: schedule model development (methodology and tool); release and iteration length (time-boxed periods in adaptive life cycles - time-boxing minimises scope creep by forcing essential features first); level of accuracy (acceptable range for realistic duration estimates, may include contingency); units of measure per resource (staff hours, days, weeks; metres, litres, tons, cubic yards); organisational procedures links (the WBS is the framework, giving consistency with estimates and schedules); schedule model maintenance (how status and progress are recorded during execution); control thresholds (agreed variation, typically % deviation from the baseline, before action is needed); rules of performance measurement (rules for percent complete, EVM techniques such as baselines, fixed-formula, percent complete; schedule measures such as SV and SPI); reporting formats and frequency.

t-6.2-define-activities.title: 6.2 Define Activities: decomposition into activities, rolling wave planning, activity list, attributes, milestones
t-6.2-define-activities.notes: Identify and document the specific actions to produce deliverables; key benefit: decomposes work packages into schedule activities as the basis for estimating, scheduling, executing, monitoring and controlling; performed throughout. Inputs: schedule management plan (methodology, rolling-wave wave duration, level of detail); scope baseline (WBS, deliverables, constraints, assumptions); EEFs (culture and structure, commercial databases, PMIS); OPAs (lessons learned with activity lists from similar projects, standardised processes, activity list templates, activity planning policies). Tools: expert judgment; decomposition - activities represent the effort to complete a work package; Define Activities produces activities whereas Create WBS produces deliverables; the activity list, WBS and WBS dictionary can be developed sequentially or concurrently; involving team members improves accuracy; rolling wave planning - iterative technique where near-term work is planned in detail and future work at a higher level; a form of progressive elaboration for work packages, planning packages and release planning in agile or waterfall; meetings. Outputs: activity list (all schedule activities with an identifier and a scope-of-work description; updated periodically under rolling wave or agile); activity attributes (evolve over time: initially ID, WBS ID, name; later description, predecessors, successors, logical relationships, leads and lags, resource requirements, imposed dates, constraints, assumptions, location, calendar, type of effort; used for scheduling and sorting in reports); milestone list (significant points or events, each mandatory - e.g., contractual - or optional - e.g., historical; milestones have zero duration); change requests (elaborating deliverables into activities after baselining may reveal work outside the baselines, processed via 4.6); plan updates (schedule baseline, cost baseline).

t-6.3-sequence-activities.title: 6.3 Sequence Activities: PDM relationship types, dependency types, leads and lags
t-6.3-sequence-activities.notes: Identify and document relationships among activities; key benefit: the logical sequence of work for the greatest efficiency given all constraints; performed throughout. Every activity except the first and last should have at least one predecessor and one successor with an appropriate logical relationship; leads/lags may be needed for a realistic schedule; converts the activity list into a diagram as a first step to the schedule baseline. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, accuracy); scope baseline; documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log - may create schedule risks, milestone list); EEFs (standards, PMIS, scheduling tools, work authorisation systems); OPAs (portfolio and program plans and dependencies, policies, network templates, lessons learned). Tools: precedence diagramming method (PDM) - activities are nodes linked by logical relationships; predecessor comes before a dependent activity, successor comes after. Finish-to-start (FS): successor cannot start until predecessor finishes (install OS after assembling the PC) - most common. Finish-to-finish (FF): successor cannot finish until predecessor finishes (editing finishes after writing finishes). Start-to-start (SS): successor cannot start until predecessor starts (level concrete after pouring begins). Start-to-finish (SF): successor cannot finish until predecessor starts (new payables system must start before the old one can shut down) - very rarely used. Two relationships between the same pair (e.g., SS and FF) are possible but not recommended - pick the highest-impact one; closed loops not recommended. Dependency determination and integration - four attributes combinable in pairs: mandatory (legally/contractually required or inherent in the work; physical limits; 'hard logic'; not to be confused with schedule constraints in the tool; technical dependencies are not necessarily mandatory) vs discretionary (preferred/preferential/soft logic based on best practice or a desired sequence, e.g., electrical after plumbing to reduce risk; document fully because they can create arbitrary total float and limit options; review when fast tracking); external (project activities vs non-project activities, usually outside team control - hardware delivery, government hearings) vs internal (between project activities, inside team control). Leads and lags: lead = time a successor can be advanced relative to its predecessor (landscaping starts 2 weeks before punch list completion = FS with a 2-week lead; often shown as negative lag in software).
